newsitem.title: RUSSIA: De Beers, ARS wary of Moscow's role in gem exports.
newsitem.headline: De Beers, ARS wary of Moscow's role in gem exports.

text.p: Russian diamond monopoly Almazy Rossii-Sakha and South Africa's De Beers said Thursday they would hold high-level talks soon to mull the next step to reaching an elusive trade deal.

At the top of the agenda will be President Boris Yeltsin's recent decree on the diamond market, which suggested the Kremlin was looking to impose more control on the lucrative diamond export business.

"We plan to hold talks in Moscow with De Beers for the preliminary discussion of documents including the recent government decree," said ARS spokesman Georgy Minayev. "Realistically it will be at the beginning of September."
ARS President Vyacheslav Shtyrov warned both sides should brace themselves for unexpected changes ahead.
"We have to be prepared for changes which may happen independently of our wish or knowledge," he was quoted by Itar-Tass news agency as saying this week.

ARS wants a new deal after De Beers sharply curtailed the amount of diamonds it bought from Russia when the last deal expired at the end of 1996. That deal was worth around $1.2 billion to Russia annually.

ARS has received a state export license covering deliveries abroad until the end of the year but soon may be forced to divide the spoils with a government exporter -- a prospect the company does not relish.

"Certainly, the appearance of two exporters is a question. I don't see how Alrosa could gain anything by this," Minayev said, using the shortened company name. "I do see that Alrosa could lose something by it."
Raymond Clarke, head of De Beers' Moscow office, said the presidential decree was a step in the right direction towards a full trade agreement with ARS, but was far from being the conclusive measure.

Both firms must now decide how a draft trade deal, first submitted late last year, fits in with the presidential order. In the meantime De Beers would continue to buy Russian gems from ARS and operate as normally as possible.

"ARS can export their diamonds to whomever they wish. We obviously hope we will get the lion's share," Clarke said, adding that a full trade deal was still preferable since it was good for the stability of the gem industry worldwide.
